headings.title: Introduction to Case-Control Studies
headings.content: A case-control study is a type of observational research used frequently in epidemiology and nursing research. It looks backward in time. Researchers start with two groups of people: those who already have a specific disease or health condition, called the **cases**, and those who do not have the condition, called the **controls**. Then, the research team asks both groups about their past exposures to find out if a certain factor caused the illness. This design is retrospective, meaning it moves from the effect back to the cause.

headings.title: Selecting Cases and Controls
headings.content: Choosing the right people for your study is critical for accurate results. The **cases** must be clearly defined using strict diagnostic criteria so that everyone in that group actually has the condition. The **controls** must come from the same population as the cases and must be completely free of the disease in question. If the control group is chosen poorly, the study results will be skewed and unreliable.

headings.title: Assessing Past Exposures
headings.content: Because case-control studies look backward, researchers must collect data on past exposures. This is often done through interviews, medical records, or questionnaires. A major challenge here is **recall bias**, which happens when sick people try harder to remember past exposures than healthy people do. To reduce this problem, researchers use standardized questionnaires and blind interviewers to the study hypothesis whenever possible.

headings.title: Measures of Association: The Odds Ratio
headings.content:
You cannot calculate actual disease incidence or relative risk directly in a case-control study because the researchers control how many cases and controls are selected. Instead, researchers use the **odds ratio (OR)**. The odds ratio compares the odds of exposure among the cases to the odds of exposure among the controls.

- **OR = 1**: Exposure does not affect the odds of disease.
- **OR > 1**: Exposure is associated with higher odds of disease (risk factor).
- **OR < 1**: Exposure is associated with lower odds of disease (protective factor).

headings.title: Confounding and Bias
headings.content: Case-control studies are prone to errors that can ruin study findings. A **confounding variable** is an outside factor that relates to both the exposure and the disease, tricking the researcher into seeing a false connection. For example, if researchers study coffee drinking and lung cancer, smoking is a confounder because coffee drinkers smoke more often. Researchers control confounding during study design by matching participants or during data analysis by using statistical adjustments.

headings.title: Advantages and Limitations
headings.content: Every research design has strong points and weak points. Case-control studies are fantastic for rare diseases because you do not have to wait years for people to get sick. They are also inexpensive and quick to complete. However, they are terrible for studying rare exposures and cannot prove cause-and-effect because they look backward from the outcome.
